headline: This law lets the first person appointed as Secretary of Defense after its passage be someone who left regular active-duty military service at least three years earlier, instead of seven.
what_it_does: Current law bars anyone from becoming Secretary of Defense within seven years after leaving active duty as a regular commissioned officer of the Armed Forces. This law creates a one-time exception. It applies only to the first person appointed to that job after the law was enacted, and that person needs only three years to have passed since leaving such active duty. The exception does not change the rule for anyone appointed later.

who_it_affects.group: The individual nominated as the first Secretary of Defense after January 20, 2017
who_it_affects.how: This person could be a recently retired regular-duty commissioned officer who had been out of active duty for at least three years rather than seven.

who_it_affects.group: Former regular-component commissioned officers of the Armed Forces
who_it_affects.how: Their eligibility for the Secretary of Defense post is affected only for the first appointment after enactment, under the shortened waiting period.

when_it_takes_effect: The exception applies on the date of enactment, January 20, 2017, and covers only the first appointment made after that date.
